chapter: New York, Henderson and Charlie Johnson
title: Henderson versus Chick Webb at the Savoy and brother Horace's stolen charts
summary: At the Savoy Henderson's band finally beat Chick Webb, who usually won because Horace Henderson sold his brother's arrangements to Webb; Autrey loved playing Fletcher's logical, comfortable writing.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money

blocks.x: Well you were -- you went out with Fletcher after the rehearsal at Fletcher's house?
Uh-huh, uh-huh.
And you said you wanted to stay with Fletcher.

Yeah. Yeah, after doing this thing we had a -- I think it was a New Year's Eve thing. We did it with Fletcher, and the band went pretty good, and where I was lucky and happy afterwards for doing this recording, and I didn't have the music, and I memorized it, and everything went well.

Well after that we had a couple of days, or one day, in the Savoy. Well for years, before -- even before I met Fletcher, or joined him, he and Chick Webb (laughs) had been battling, you know, and music, you know, who's the best, who's greatest, and when the people would pack the place to see it. So while I was with him he's saying we had a -- oh, strenuous rehearsal. He said well I'm going to play against that little guy again. He said this time I must -- I gotta get -- I gotta get him.
I said who? He said Chick Webb. I said all right,

nice, you know. I was for it. I had never played against Chick, and I knew Chick. I knew him, naturally, as much as I knew about him. I knew about Chick and both, because I'd been hearing about them for years. So we get to the Savoy. The place is packed. Ohhh, you never saw so many people. And Fletcher's playing -- you know, Fletcher had something with that beat, dunh dee, dee, pa-daddle doo dee duh duh dum, bah bee, dah dah jussle, and look out and he'd see the people. You'd see the heads bouncing.
(Laughter.)

You see hundreds of hundreds of people on the floor, and they were bouncing in the beat, and it made you feel good. And -- well, Fletcher had always had this problem, when everything he played against Chick before, his brother Horace, who would steal his arrangements, and sell them to Chick.
(Laughter.)
As his absense, of course, so when you get on the job, instead of him playing something that Chick hadn't heard, Chick would beat him to it and play it before he heard it.
(Laughter.)
And most times, played better. That's how good Chick's band -- oh, Chick had a heck of a band! Oh man! And the band would play it, and Fletcher would say How
did they get that? That'sounds like one of my things!
(Laughter.)

You know? And Chick would be -- all -- well, when you buy it, and Horace would sell it and make him some money. Horace could play very nice piano himself, but he was still a stinker. He was -- steals his brothers things and sell it, you know. (Laughs.) Wow!

So we would sit there and play, and I had never played any of the arrangements like Fletcher's in my life, you know, I was so elated I was just knocked out, because he would -- he would bring his hands down, and the band would start the rhythm, uh-one, two, three, four, one, two, three, four, and you stayed there, and you didn't have to move, and it was no -- you were comfortable, just play. And then those were there, I mean you didn't have to look -- to me, you didn't have to worry about reading, because everything was there, and it was-- the way he wrote, that was the way he wrote music.
And --
You mean he was logical?
Oh, logical, oh man, it was so pleasing, them things were so nice.

So at the end, Fletcher jumped and screamed and said at last! At last I've got him! Because for years they had been doing that, and Chick had been winning out, you know? At last I got him! I got him! I got -- you know. And -- but
I mean everybody was happy, and people enjoyed the music, and we got paid, and Fletcher was happy. But Chick had been winning for so many years it didn't matter.
